text:
“Turning Dross Into Gold Loss” replaces SASRec’s one-negative BCE with full-catalog cross-entropy or uncorrected sampled cross-entropy: loss = logsumexp([positive_score, negative_scores]) − positive_score. Sample N unseen items separately for each user sequence, then reuse that user’s negatives across every valid timestep. This is sharing within a sequence, rather than one batch-wide pool or independent negatives per timestep. The paper reports strong results with 3,000 negatives; its equations contain no logQ correction. [Paper, §3](https://arxiv.org/html/2309.07602v1)

Implementation guidance: exclude padding ID 0 and all items in the available training history, including shifted positive targets; never inspect held-out interactions for training exclusions. Uniform rejection sampling produces uniform draws over eligible items. Rejection with replacement can produce duplicates; enforcing uniqueness gives sampling without replacement and requires N ≤ eligible catalog size. The paper calls negatives a “set” but does not establish duplicate handling in its prose; repository sampler behavior was not verified. Duplicates retained in logits count repeatedly in the denominator. For a shared batch pool, user-specific masking is necessary; masking without replenishment leaves different effective negative counts. These are implementation consequences, not verified author-code details.

For reproducing this sampled candidate-classification objective, use ordinary cross-entropy with target column zero and average over nonpadding targets; no correction is required. Approximating full-catalog softmax is a different objective: uniformity alone does not justify dropping every correction, because the positive is always included while negatives are sampled. Subtracting an identical constant from every candidate cancels, whereas correcting only sampled negatives changes the loss. History exclusion also removes support needed to estimate an unrestricted full-catalog denominator. [LogQ analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.09331)
